text: Marguerite heard the post-hole digger before she saw it, a grinding thud that came up through the kitchen floor and into the soles of her slippers. She set the kettle down without pouring. Through the gap in the curtains she could see Dale Pruitt in his orange vest, the same man who had kicked her cat across the driveway in June and told her, smiling, that accidents happen to old ladies who live alone. He was driving stakes a full yard onto her side of the line. Her phone was in her hand before she remembered dialing anything, and then she could not decide who to call. The police had come last time and left after ten minutes. When he glanced toward the window she dropped below the sill so fast her knee cracked against the radiator. She stayed crouched there, breath whistling through her nose, listening to the hammer strike again and again, each blow closer to the hydrangeas her husband had planted. She did not get up until the light outside went orange, and even then she kept the lamps off.

The surveyor folded his map on the hood of his truck and said, very carefully, that the property line ran about four feet west of where we all thought it did. I laughed, because that would put the line straight through my garage. He didn't laugh back. My neighbor, Corinne, who only wanted a nice cedar fence for her dogs, went pale and started apologizing as if she had done something. I kept doing the math in my head. Four feet. The garage. The mortgage I refinanced in March, the one the bank only approved because of the appraisal. My mouth went dry and I could hear my pulse in my ears like a dripping tap. I asked him to measure again and my voice came out too high, too fast. He said he could, but the pins were original, and the county records matched. I walked inside and sat on the edge of the bathtub with the door locked and my hands pressed flat on my thighs to stop them shaking. Somewhere a lawyer was going to tell me what this cost, and I already knew I could not pay it.

Tomasz held the utility map up to the morning light and traced the yellow dashed line with his thumb. Gas main. Right where his neighbor Ruth wanted the new fence posts to go, eighteen inches down, according to a drawing nobody had updated since 1987. Ruth's contractor was already unloading the auger from his trailer, whistling. Tomasz's stomach turned over. His brother had been a lineman; he had heard the stories about crews who hit a line and what was left of the trench afterward. He jogged across the lawn, waving both arms, his voice cracking when he shouted for them to wait. The contractor shrugged and said they always dig shallow first. Tomasz could not stop picturing the auger biting into steel, the hiss, the spark from a stone. He stood between the machine and the stakes, heart slamming, and refused to move until someone called the utility hotline. Even after the man grudgingly dialed, Tomasz kept glancing at his own house, at his daughter's bedroom window directly behind the line, measuring the distance in strides.

The letter about the fence had been taped to my door instead of mailed, and the tape was the kind used for packing boxes, wrapped three times around. Inside, my new neighbor had written that he would be building a seven-foot barrier along our shared line and that I should keep my kids away from it. Then, underlined twice: I know what you did at your last address. I read it standing in the hallway with my coat still on. I had never met this man. I had moved here specifically so that no one knew anything about me, about the divorce, about the restraining order I had filed against my ex. My fingers went cold and stiff around the paper. I checked the deadbolt, then checked it again. I pulled the blinds in the children's room and moved Amara's bed away from the window without telling her why. All evening I kept hearing his hammer through the wall, steady and patient, and each time it stopped I held my breath, waiting for footsteps on the porch.

Ifeoma was nine and she knew the fence meant Biscuit would be stuck on the other side. The Hendersons' dog was huge and had a bark like a car crash, and the new fence was going to have a gate with a spring latch that the grown-ups said could not possibly come open. But she had seen it come open. She had watched it swing wide in the wind yesterday while Mr. Henderson was on the phone. Now she stood at the end of the driveway with her backpack straps clenched in both fists, unable to make her legs carry her past the gap where the gate was hung. Her chest felt like it had a balloon inside it, getting bigger. Every rustle in the hedge made her flinch and step back onto the curb. When the school bus turned the corner she did not run to it the way she usually did. She waited until the driver honked twice, then sprinted the whole way with her eyes squeezed nearly shut, and she did not breathe out until the doors folded closed behind her.

Hollis had been rehearsing the conversation for three days and still his voice shook when he finally knocked on Gerald's door. The man had a rifle rack in the back window of his truck and a habit of standing in his yard at night, smoking, watching. Hollis only wanted to ask whether the fence could stop at the old oak instead of cutting through his vegetable beds. When Gerald opened the door, he did not say hello. He just filled the frame, waiting. Hollis felt sweat collect under his collar despite the cold. He stammered through the request, words tripping over each other, and his eyes kept sliding toward the dark hallway behind the big man, toward the shape of something leaning against the wall. Gerald said nothing for a long time. Then he said he would think about it, in a tone that made the hair rise on Hollis's arms. Walking back across the frozen grass, Hollis felt the man's gaze on the back of his neck like a hand, and he did not dare turn around until his own door was locked.

The envelope was thick and cream-colored, with the property management company's logo in the corner, and Rosalind knew before she opened it. She had been two weeks late in September and three in October. She sat on the stairwell step outside her unit because her legs would not take her the rest of the way inside. The words swam: notice to vacate, thirty days, failure to comply. Thirty days. She did the arithmetic again and again, the same numbers each time. Her daughter's school was four blocks away. Every other apartment she had looked at was across the river, or needed first, last, and a deposit she did not have. Her throat closed up and she pressed the back of her wrist to her mouth so the neighbors would not hear the sound that came out. Downstairs a door slammed and she jumped, shoving the letter into her coat as though someone might snatch it. When she finally went in, she stood in the doorway of her daughter's room, watching her sleep, and could not make herself let go of the doorframe.

My landlord doesn't send letters. He sends texts with too many exclamation points, or he just shows up. So when an actual letter came, certified, signature required, I stood at the mailbox with the pen hovering over the carrier's tablet for a long, stupid moment. The carrier looked at me like she'd seen that hesitation before. Inside, it said the building had been sold, effective immediately, and that all tenants should expect an inspection of their units by the new owners on Thursday. Thursday. I thought about the room at the back, the one I've been letting my cousin Mateo sleep in since he lost his job, the one that is definitely not on my lease. I thought about his papers, or rather the lack of them. My hands started to sweat so badly the paper went soft. I walked upstairs slowly, counting the steps, trying to figure out how to tell him, trying to figure out where he could possibly go in three days, and every car that slowed down outside made my shoulders jerk up toward my ears.

The note under Wen's door was handwritten, not printed, and the handwriting slanted hard to the left. It said the landlord would be entering the apartment on Saturday to perform repairs, and that she did not need to be present. She read that last part four times. She had never asked for repairs. The lock on her door was one the landlord had keys to; she had asked to change it twice and been told no. Last month she had come home and found the bathroom light on when she was certain she had turned it off, and the toilet seat up. She lived alone. Now she sat on her bed with her knees pulled to her chest and her phone in her hand, the screen lit with her sister's number, thumb not quite pressing. Every creak in the hallway sent a jolt through her ribs. She got up, wedged a kitchen chair under the doorknob, and then sat facing the door with the lights on, listening, until the windows started to turn grey with morning.

I was halfway through my cereal when I noticed the letter had my name spelled wrong. Not my real name, the one on my documents, but the one I gave the landlord when I signed. Kwame Mensah. No one in this city knew me as anything else. Except this letter said it was regarding a background check requested by the new lease compliance office, and it used my actual surname, the one I left behind with everything else. The spoon slid from my fingers and clattered in the bowl. I read the sentence again, and again, and the letters didn't change. Somebody had found the old name. Somebody had connected it to this address. My heart was going so fast it felt like it was skipping rather than beating. I went to the window and looked down at the street, scanning parked cars for anyone sitting inside them. Then I started pulling clothes out of drawers, not folding them, just stuffing them into the duffel bag under the bed, while my mind kept racing through who might have told them.

Eighty-one years old, and Dorothea had lived in apartment 4C since the Carter administration. The letter from the new landlord was polite, almost cheerful, explaining that the building would be undergoing renovation and that long-term tenants were encouraged to consider relocation packages. She held it close to her face under the lamp because her glasses were not strong enough anymore. Relocation. To where? Her doctor was across the street. The pharmacist knew her by name. Her son was in Phoenix and had not called since Easter. She put the letter down and picked it up again, and her hand trembled so much that the paper rattled. There was a tightness spreading across her chest and she sat very still, wondering whether this was the kind she should call someone about. The radiator knocked, and she jumped. She kept thinking about the woman from 2A who took a package and moved to a place out in the county, and how nobody ever heard from her again, and how her plants had died on the windowsill before the movers came.

Ravi saw the landlord's letter sitting on the mat and immediately looked at the ceiling, at the brown stain that had been spreading for six weeks, the one that bulged now like a blister. He had reported it three times. The letter said the landlord had received an engineering report on the building's roof structure and that tenants on the top floor should avoid using the rear bedroom until further notice. Further notice. He had been sleeping in that bedroom. His twins slept in the cot against the far wall. He went in without turning on the light and stood under the stain, and in the quiet he could hear something he had been telling himself was the pipes: a slow, groaning creak, like a ship. His scalp prickled. He scooped up both babies at once, awkwardly, one under each arm, and backed out of the room without taking his eyes off the ceiling. Then he shut the door, pressed his back against it, and stood in the hallway breathing hard, holding them so tightly that one of them began to fuss.

The board had flipped from DELAYED to SEE AGENT, and the agent was not saying anything useful. Beatriz stood at the counter gripping the strap of her bag with both hands. Her father's surgery was at seven the next morning in Lisbon, and the doctors had been clear that if it went badly, the hours before would be the last good ones. She had promised him on the phone that she would be there to hold his hand when he went under. Now the agent was typing and frowning and typing again, and saying something about a crew timing out. Beatriz felt her throat lock up. She asked whether there was another flight and heard her own voice crack halfway through the question. The man behind her sighed loudly. She kept checking her phone every few seconds, as if a message from her brother might somehow appear saying everything had already gone wrong. Her knees felt unreliable. When the agent finally looked up and shook his head, she had to put a hand flat on the counter to stay standing.

The delay itself didn't bother me. What bothered me was the reason. The pilot came over the intercom, after we'd already been sitting on the tarmac for forty minutes, and said in a very flat voice that maintenance had identified an issue with one of the engines and that they were going to try a fix. Try. I hate flying even on a good day. I looked out the window at the wing and the engine casing and the two men in vests standing beneath it, one of them shaking his head. My palms were wet against the armrests. The woman next to me, a teacher named Gail, said cheerfully that they'd never let us take off if it weren't safe, and I nodded, but I couldn't swallow properly. When they announced an hour later that the problem was resolved and we would be departing shortly, the cabin applauded. I didn't. I was staring at the men under the wing, at the one who was still shaking his head as he walked back toward the hangar.

Five hours into the delay, the gate area had thinned out, and Yusuf realized the man in the grey hoodie had not left. He had been three seats away at gate B12, then two rows behind at the cafe, and now he was leaning against the pillar near the restrooms, not looking at his phone, not looking at the departure board. Just looking at Yusuf. Yusuf was carrying his company's prototype in the hard case between his ankles, and his boss had warned him, half joking, about people who would pay a lot to see what was inside. He pulled the case closer with his feet. His mouth tasted metallic. He tried to act normal, opening a book he could not read, turning pages he had not seen. When he got up to find a security officer, the man in the hoodie straightened too. Yusuf's heartbeat thudded so hard he could feel it in his teeth. He walked faster, then made himself slow down, then sped up again, the case banging against his shin.

Each time they pushed the departure back another hour, I counted the pills in my bag again. Six. Enough for today, but not tomorrow, because I'd packed for a two-hour flight and not for this, whatever this was, a storm system over Denver and no rebooking until morning. My seizure medication isn't something you can buy at an airport pharmacy, and the one in terminal C closed at nine. I sat on the floor near an outlet with my back against the wall and tried to keep my breathing slow. I kept feeling for that aura, that flicker at the edge of my vision, and every time the fluorescent lights buzzed I thought it was starting. My name is Siobhan, I'm thirty-four, and I have not had one in public since college, and I was not prepared to have one on the dirty carpet of gate C9 surrounded by strangers. I called my neurologist's after-hours line and got a recording. I hung up and held my phone against my chest, both hands, like it could do something.

Little Ahanu had been holding his grandmother's hand all through the long delay, and then in the crush at the gate change he wasn't. He was six. He looked up and there were only legs and rolling suitcases and a huge window full of planes, and none of the coats were her green one. He turned in a circle, then another. His breath started coming in hiccups. He did not know the name of the city they were going to, only that it had snow and his cousins. A loudspeaker said something long and booming that he could not understand. He backed up against a pillar and pressed himself flat against it, trying to be small, his lower lip shaking so hard his teeth chattered. A woman in a uniform bent down and asked where his mommy was, and he could not make any words come out at all, just a thin squeak. He clutched the strap of his backpack and stared past her, searching every green thing in the crowd, every single one, until his eyes burned.

Constance watched the news crawl beneath the departure screen at gate 22: protests near the capital, airport closures possible, foreign nationals advised to shelter in place. Her flight out had been delayed twice already and now showed no time at all, just a dash. Around her, conversations dropped into whispers in a language she only half understood. Two soldiers walked past the gate, rifles slung, and everyone went quiet until they had gone. Her passport was in her inside pocket; she touched it through her jacket every few minutes, feeling for the hard rectangle. Her phone was at eleven percent. She had texted her husband that everything was fine, and that lie sat in her stomach like a stone. When a sound echoed from somewhere beyond the terminal, a dull crack, half the gate stood up at once. Constance did not stand. She bent forward over her knees and made herself as compact as possible, her heart racing, eyes fixed on the exit sign, already planning which way she would run.

The nurse said the doctor would like to go over the results in person, and Gideon knew what that meant. Good news comes in the portal. Good news is a green checkmark. He drove to the clinic with the radio off, and twice he missed a turn because he was staring at nothing. In the waiting room he picked up a magazine and held it without reading, his thumb working a crease into the cover. His wife had wanted to come and he had told her not to bother, and now he wished more than anything that she was beside him. When the door opened and someone called his name, his legs felt like they belonged to another man. The exam room was cold. Dr. Abara came in holding a folder, and she sat down instead of standing, and she pulled her chair closer, and Gideon felt the floor tilt. He gripped the edge of the paper-covered table so hard it tore. His mouth opened to ask the question and nothing came out but air.

I've opened the email four times and closed it four times without scrolling down. Biopsy results available. That's all the subject line says. My mother had the same lump at the same age, same side, and I remember the year after, the wig on the stand by her bed, the smell of the hospital on her clothes. I'm sitting in the car in the grocery store parking lot because I couldn't make myself go in. My coffee has gone cold in the cup holder. My heart is hammering in this odd lopsided way, and there's a sour taste rising in the back of my throat. My name is Lucia, I'm forty-two, I have two boys who still need me to sign permission slips, and I can't move my thumb down a screen. A shopping cart rolls past and bumps the bumper and I yelp out loud. I put the phone face down on the passenger seat and press both palms against the steering wheel, and I count to fifty, and I pick it up again, and my hand won't stop shaking long enough to read.

The genetic counselor slid the paper across the desk and Henrik saw the word positive before he saw anything else. Huntington's. His father had died of it at fifty-three, after years of jerking limbs and blank rages and finally not knowing his own son's face. Henrik was thirty. He heard the counselor talking about support groups, about planning, about how a result is not a timeline, but her voice sounded like it was coming through a wall. He looked down at his hands on his knees and watched them, waiting for one of them to twitch on its own. His breath went shallow and quick. He thought of his father strapped to the chair so he would not fall, of the noises he made at night. Henrik's whole body felt cold, the way it did when he jumped into the fjord as a boy. He asked whether there was any chance of error, and he heard how pathetic it sounded, and he asked it again anyway, his voice gone thin and childish, while the counselor quietly pushed a box of tissues toward him.

The pediatrician kept smiling, which was somehow worse. She said the blood work showed some numbers they wanted to look at more closely, and that it was probably nothing, and that they had already called ahead to the children's hospital so Noa could be seen today. Today. Shira looked over at her daughter, who was coloring a purple horse on the back of a pamphlet, legs swinging off the exam table, humming. Shira's own legs felt like water. She tried to ask what numbers, which ones, how high, and her voice came out in a whisper. The doctor said the word oncology very gently, as if softness might make it lighter. Shira's vision narrowed to a tunnel with her daughter at the end of it. She stood, sat back down, stood again. Her hands kept fussing with Noa's hair, smoothing it, tucking it behind her ear over and over. In the parking garage she buckled the car seat three times, checking the straps, because she could not think of anything else her hands could do.

I'm an ER nurse. I read scans all day. So when the radiology report for my own chest CT landed in the patient app at two in the morning, I made the mistake of reading it myself. Spiculated mass, right upper lobe, 3.1 centimeters. Mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Recommend tissue sampling. I know exactly what each of those words means, and I know what they mean together, and I know the survival curves I've glanced at on posters in the break room. I sat on the edge of the bed in the dark while my husband, Tobias, slept beside me, and I felt every breath I took as if I could feel the thing in there, sitting in the top of my lung. My skin went clammy. I went to the bathroom and turned on the faucet so he wouldn't hear me, and I sat on the cold tile floor with my knees pulled up, and I tried to remember the last time I had told him anything important, and I couldn't stop my teeth from chattering even though the room was warm.

Abuelo Ernesto did not trust doctors and did not trust envelopes, and this was both. He set the letter from the clinic on the kitchen table and walked a slow circle around it, twice, as if it might spring at him. His granddaughter Paloma was at school; she usually read the hard English for him. He could make out some words. Abnormal. Follow-up. Urgent. That last one he knew very well. His heart started doing the skipping thing it did lately, the thing that had sent him to the clinic in the first place, and he lowered himself into a chair and pressed two fingers against his wrist the way the nurse had shown him, counting, losing count, starting over. Outside a dog barked and he jerked so hard the chair scraped. He thought about his wife, about how fast it had been with her, a Tuesday and then a Friday and then nothing. He did not open the envelope further. He just sat there with his hand flat on top of it, holding it down, until he heard Paloma's key in the lock.

Mr. Okafor handed the exams back face down, row by row, and Priyanka watched him get closer the way you watch a wave you can't outrun. Her scholarship required a B in chemistry, and her midterm had been a C-minus, and her father had already said, very quietly, what would happen if she lost the scholarship: she'd come home, transfer to the community college, and work at the shop with him. His quietness was always worse than shouting. When the paper landed on her desk, she did not turn it over. She pressed her palm against it and felt her pulse throbbing in her fingertips against the page. Her stomach was a hard knot. The boy beside her whooped at his grade and she flinched. She lifted one corner, just enough to see the red ink, and her vision swam so badly she couldn't make out the number. She put it back down. She stared at the clock above the board, watching the second hand jerk forward, and could not make herself breathe all the way in.

The professor didn't hand mine back. He handed everyone else theirs, and then he said, without looking up, Mr. Delacroix, please see me after class. Thirty heads turned. I felt the blood drain from my face so fast my ears rang. I knew why. Of course I knew why. The take-home essay. The paragraph I'd lifted from a blog at three in the morning, and changed, but maybe not enough. The honor code was on the first page of the syllabus in bold: one violation, expulsion. My student visa depends on enrollment. Without it I have sixty days to leave the country. For the rest of the lecture I could not take a single note. My pen kept slipping in my sweaty fingers. I watched the clock and every minute it moved was a minute closer to that door. When the class emptied out, I stayed in my seat, my legs refusing to stand, staring at my backpack zipper and gripping it as though I might still somehow grab my things and run.

Eleven-year-old Jonah saw the note stapled to the top of his math test before he saw the grade: Please have a parent sign and return. He knew what his stepfather did with notes from school. The last time, the belt had come off before Jonah's mother could even get between them. All through lunch he kept the test folded in his pocket, his hand pressed over it, feeling it crinkle. He did not eat. His throat felt too narrow for food. In the bathroom he unfolded it and stared at the 54 circled in red and the staple and the empty line for the signature, and his hands shook so badly the paper rattled. He thought about forging it. He thought about losing it. He thought about not going home, about the bus stop, about where else a person could go. When the final bell rang, he was the last one out of the building, walking so slowly the crossing guard asked if he was sick, and he said yes, because his stomach was cramping so hard he almost believed it.

Grades for the bar prep diagnostic were posted on the wall outside the dean's office, by student number, the way it used to be done fifty years ago. Matilde pushed through the cluster of people with her heart pounding so loud she was sure the others could hear it. She had taken out two hundred thousand dollars in loans for this degree. She had told her whole village back in the Azores that she would be the first lawyer in the family. Her eyes ran down the column of numbers. Her own number swam in and out of focus. The score next to it was red-flagged. Bottom decile. Strongly advised to meet with academic support. Matilde stepped back so fast she bumped into someone and did not apologize. Her chest felt tight, as if the air had gotten thick. She walked down the hallway very fast, then into a stairwell, and leaned against the cold concrete with her eyes closed, palms flat on the wall behind her, while the numbers kept stacking in her head: the loans, the interest, the years.

I got my biology final back and it was an A, which should have been fine, except that the teacher had written across the top: This answer key was missing from my desk on Thursday. Come see me. I didn't take it. I swear I didn't take it. But I had been the last person in the room on Thursday, staying late to finish my lab write-up, and Ms. Varga had seen me there, and now there was a hot prickling sensation crawling up the back of my neck. I'm already on probation from the thing last spring, the fight that wasn't my fault either. One more and it's a suspension, and a suspension means I lose my spot on the varsity team and maybe the recruiter from the state school stops calling. My name is Darnell and nobody ever believes me the first time. I sat through the rest of the period staring at my hands, which wouldn't stop jittering on the desk. When the bell rang I stood up too fast and knocked my chair over, and the whole class turned to look at me.

The flight instructor tossed the written exam onto the table in the briefing room and tapped a single question with his pen. Emergency procedures, engine fire on climbout. Svetlana had gotten it wrong. Not a little wrong. She had reversed two steps, and in a real cockpit that reversal would have fed fuel to the flames. Her checkride was in four days. She stared at the red X and felt her insides drop as though the floor had gone out from under her chair. She could see it: the smoke filling the windscreen, her fingers fumbling the mixture knob, the ground rising. She had been flying for eight months and had felt brave every time, and now she suddenly could not remember why. Her mouth was so dry her tongue stuck to the roof of it. The instructor said something about reviewing with her this afternoon. She nodded without hearing, hands knotted together in her lap until the knuckles went white, and kept seeing the fire, and her own hands doing the wrong thing, again and again.

Fiona was reaching for a bag of lemons when she heard her old name, the one nobody had called her in eleven years. She turned and there was Cheryl, from the commune, from the farm in Oregon, smiling the same wide smile with a basket over her arm. Fiona's whole body locked. She remembered that smile across the dinner table while the leader decided who would be punished. She remembered how Cheryl had been the one who reported people. Cheryl said how wonderful, what a coincidence, did she live nearby? Fiona heard herself say no, just passing through, her voice brittle and too bright. Her fingers had closed around a lemon so tightly that juice was seeping from the peel. Cheryl said some of the old family had been asking about her. Family. The word went through Fiona like cold water. She mumbled something about being late and walked away without her cart, past the registers, out into the parking lot, and drove three different routes home, watching the mirror the entire time.

I knew it was Ollie before he turned around. Same hunched shoulders, same habit of tapping his foot while reading the back of a cereal box. We'd been inseparable at twenty, and then there was the night with the car, and the boy on the bicycle, and the agreement we'd made in the gas station bathroom with our hands still shaking. We never told anyone. We never spoke again. Now he looked up and saw me, and his face went through about five things at once before landing on a smile that didn't reach his eyes. My stomach turned over. He walked over slowly and said, quietly, that a detective had come by his place last week asking about that summer. My ears started ringing. The fluorescent lights seemed suddenly too bright, the aisle too narrow. I asked what he'd told them and my voice was barely a whisper. He looked at me for a long moment and didn't answer. Behind us a stock boy dropped a crate and we both jumped, and I saw that his hands were trembling exactly as badly as mine.

Bartholomew spotted Desmond by the deli counter and his first instinct was to wave, and then he saw the man standing just behind his old friend, tall, with a shaved head and a tattoo creeping up out of his collar. Desmond's eyes met his and widened, and Desmond gave the smallest shake of his head. No. Don't. Bartholomew's hand stopped halfway up. He knew that Desmond had gotten mixed up with some people after the factory closed; he had heard it secondhand. He had not known it looked like this, Desmond pale and sweating in the frozen-food chill, the big man's hand resting on his shoulder like a clamp. Bartholomew's pulse began to pound in his throat. He pretended to read a jar of pickles, staring at the label without understanding a word. Should he call someone? Would that make it worse? When he dared to look up again they were walking toward the exit together, and Desmond glanced back once, a look so naked that Bartholomew had to grab the edge of the shelf to steady himself.

My best friend from high school, Annika, hugged me between the bread aisle and the bakery, and over her shoulder I saw him. Lars. Her husband. The one who put me in the hospital two years ago when I helped her leave him the first time. She had gone back. I'd heard, but I hadn't believed it. Now he was walking toward us with a carton of milk in one hand and that easy grin, and every muscle in my back drew tight as a wire. Annika's arms around me had gone stiff too. She whispered in my ear, so quietly I almost missed it, please just go. Lars said my name like we were old pals. My voice came out cracked when I answered. I could feel the scar under my hair start to throb, the way it does in the cold. I backed away, smiling a terrible fake smile, my cart bumping a display of rolls, and I didn't stop walking until I was in my car with the doors locked and the engine running, gasping like I'd been underwater.

Mrs. Takahashi recognized Eiko at once, even after forty years, even with the white hair. They had been girls together in Hiroshima prefecture, and then Eiko had moved away, and that was that. But when Eiko came closer and said, so warmly, Michiko, how wonderful, how is your husband, Michiko felt the world wobble. Her husband. Her husband was dead. Wasn't he? She had been to the funeral. Hadn't she? She could not remember the funeral. She could not remember, suddenly, what she had come here to buy, or which car was hers, or whether she had driven at all. The doctor had used a word last month, and her son had gone very quiet in the car afterward. Michiko's hands began to tremble around the handle of the basket. She smiled at Eiko and nodded and said fine, he is fine, while inside her chest something was fluttering wildly, a bird in a closed room. When Eiko left she stood in the cereal aisle for a very long time, not moving, unable to choose a single direction to step in.

Twenty years ago I left this town owing Rocco Benedetti eleven thousand dollars and a promise. I'm back for one weekend, for my aunt's funeral, and I only stopped at the Food King because she always bought her coffee there. Rocco was at the end of the produce aisle, heavier and greyer, and when he saw me he set down a cantaloupe very slowly. He said, Vinnie. That's all. Just my name. My mouth went dry as chalk. I could feel my heartbeat in my fingertips around the cart handle. He started walking toward me, not fast, and I swear the store got quieter. I started talking before he even got close, babbling about my aunt, about how I always meant to call, about how I could send something next month, and my voice kept cracking like a kid's. He stopped right in front of me and looked at my cart and at my shaking hands and at my face, and he didn't say anything for so long that I thought my knees were going to fold right there by the tomatoes.

The engine died on the overpass, in the middle lane, at rush hour. Nadia felt the steering go heavy in her hands and the dashboard light up like a carnival, and then the car was coasting, slowing, stopping, while a semi bore down in the rearview mirror. She jammed the hazards on. Horns blared on both sides. Trucks thundered past so close that the car rocked, and every time one did she flinched as if struck. Her seatbelt felt like it was choking her. She knew the advice: get out, get behind the barrier. But to get out she would have to open her door into a river of traffic going seventy. She sat frozen, gripping the dead wheel, watching the mirror, watching another set of headlights grow and grow and swerve away at the last second. Her breath came in short gasps that fogged the window. She fumbled for her phone and dropped it in the footwell. When she bent to grab it, a horn screamed beside her so loudly that she cried out and clapped both hands over her ears.

I was on the shortcut through the canyon when the car coughed, shuddered, and rolled to a stop on the gravel shoulder. No signal. Of course no signal. The nearest town was twenty miles back. I told myself somebody would come along, and somebody did: an old pickup, slowing, then stopping about fifty yards ahead. It just sat there, idling, the brake lights red. Nobody got out. I could see the shape of a man in the driver's seat, and he was not moving, and I realized he was watching me in his side mirror. My skin went cold despite the heat coming off the asphalt. I'm a pharmacist named Celeste and I have never once thought of myself as someone who needed to be careful, and now I locked all four doors with a thunk that sounded impossibly loud. The truck sat there. Two minutes. Five. My hand found the tire iron under the passenger seat, and I held it in my lap, knuckles white, eyes fixed on those red lights, not blinking, barely breathing.

Smoke. That was what Haruto noticed first, a thin grey wisp curling up from under the hood of the old Corolla as he idled at the light on Fifth. Then the smell, acrid and hot, and the temperature gauge pinned at the top. He wrenched the wheel and bumped up onto the curb in front of a laundromat. The smoke thickened, then darkened, and a flicker of orange appeared at the seam of the hood. His four-year-old was buckled in the back. Haruto's fingers tore at his own seatbelt and the buckle would not release. He pressed again, again, his thumb slipping. His breath was a high whine in his throat. When it finally gave, he threw himself out and yanked at the rear door, and the child-lock caught, and he had to run around to the other side, slipping on the wet curb. Kenji was crying now. Haruto fumbled with the car seat straps, his hands so clumsy they felt borrowed, and when he finally hauled his son free he kept running, holding him, until they were across the street and halfway down the block.

The car stalled on the railroad crossing. Ingrid would remember that sentence later as if it were the opening of a story she had read, but in the moment there was only the engine dying, the key twisting and producing nothing but a click, and the red lights on the crossing arm beginning to blink. Ding. Ding. Ding. The arm came down across the hood with a soft thump. She looked left down the tracks and saw the light, far off but growing. She turned the key again. Click. Her mouth opened and a sound came out that she did not recognize as her own voice. Her fingers fumbled for the door handle and could not find it, then found it and pulled, and the door would not open because the arm was in the way. She threw her shoulder against it. The horn of the train sounded, long and enormous, and the whole car vibrated with it. She scrambled across the console to the passenger side, kicking, her coat snagging on the gearshift, sobbing without tears.

It's not the breakdown that has me sweating in the cold. It's the time. I'm sitting on the shoulder of Route 9 with the hood up and the tow truck forty-five minutes out, and it's 8:20, and my parole officer's office is across town and my check-in is at nine. The paperwork is very clear about missed check-ins. My PO has been clear too, last time, in a tone that left no room for argument. I've called the office three times. Voicemail. I've texted the number on the card. Nothing. I'm pacing back and forth beside the car, Kofi, twenty-six, eleven months clean and employed, and I'm thinking about the cell, the green paint, the noise at night. My chest feels tight like someone's sitting on it. I keep checking the phone, then the road, then the phone again. A cop car passes and slows and every muscle in my body locks up until it speeds up again. I try calling once more and my thumb is shaking so badly I hit the wrong number twice.

The snow was coming sideways when the car slid into the ditch and stopped with a lurch. Augustin cranked the key until the starter whined and died, and then there was nothing but wind and the tick of cooling metal. The dashboard said minus nineteen outside. He had no blanket, no shovel, only the thin wool coat he wore to the office and a half bottle of water. He tried his phone: one bar, flickering, then none. He knew enough to stay with the car. He also knew the stories, the ones in the paper every winter, about people found in the spring. The cold began creeping in through the floorboards almost immediately, through his dress shoes, into his toes. His breath clouded the windshield. Every few minutes he scraped a hole in the frost to look for headlights, and every time there were none, his heart thudded harder against his ribs. He started talking aloud to himself, counting things, the buttons on his coat, the seconds between gusts, anything to keep his mind off how badly his fingers had begun to hurt.

Curfew was midnight, and it was now 2:14, and Lena had stopped pretending to read. The book lay closed in her lap. Her son's phone went straight to voicemail, the cheerful recorded greeting he had made at fourteen, and she had heard it eleven times now. Every set of headlights that swept across the living room ceiling brought her half out of the chair, and every one passed by. She had called his friend Brody's house and gotten Brody's mother, groggy and confused, saying Brody was asleep and had been home since ten. So where was Sami? Lena's hands had gone cold and she kept rubbing them on her thighs. She went to the window. She came back. She checked the hospital's number on her phone and did not call it, because calling it would make it real. Somewhere far off a siren rose and faded, and she followed the sound with her whole body, standing rigid in the middle of the rug, holding her breath until it was gone.

I saw the post on the neighborhood app at 1:30 in the morning while I was waiting up for Theo. Shots fired near the park on Halsey. Multiple people running. Theo said he was going to a party on Halsey. I called him and it rang, and rang, and rang, and went to voicemail. I called again. I texted in all capitals, something I've never done in my life. Then I just stood in the kitchen with the phone held out in front of me in both hands like an offering, staring at it, willing it to light up. My heart was going so fast I felt dizzy. My husband came downstairs and asked what was wrong and I couldn't form the words; I just turned the screen toward him. He went white and grabbed the car keys. I followed him to the door in my socks, then realized someone had to be here if Theo came home, and so I stood in the doorway, shivering in the cold, watching our taillights disappear around the corner, and everything inside me was screaming his name.

Ngozi found her daughter's bedroom window open at midnight, the screen pushed out and lying in the flowerbed below. The bed was made, which was the strangest part; Adaeze never made her bed. On the pillow was nothing. No note. Ngozi's breath hitched, and she put a hand on the windowsill to steady herself and felt the cold air pouring in. She thought of the older boy with the black car that had idled outside the school last week, the one Adaeze had sworn she didn't know. She went through her daughter's desk with clumsy fingers, pulling out drawers, looking for anything. A charger. Gum wrappers. A receipt from a gas station two towns over. Her legs started to shake so badly she had to sit on the edge of the bed. She tried the girl's phone and heard it buzzing, faintly, from under the pillow. Left behind. Ngozi pressed the vibrating phone to her chest and rocked forward and back, forward and back, and when she finally dialed the police her voice was so thin the dispatcher had to ask her to repeat everything twice.

The roads had iced over by eleven, and my daughter Maren had taken the car to her shift at the diner out on the county road, the one with the curve by the reservoir. She'd texted at 10:52: leaving now. That was over an hour ago. It's a twenty-minute drive. I've been standing at the front window with the curtain pulled back so long my arm aches. The weather radio on the counter keeps repeating its warning about black ice in that same flat robot voice. I keep picturing that curve. The guardrail that's been broken since August. The water underneath, black, half-frozen. My stomach is a cold fist. I've called her six times, and it rings out each time, and I tell myself she's driving, she's being careful, she wouldn't pick up while driving. I put on my boots and coat. I take them off. I put them on again and grab the flashlight and stand by the door with my hand on the knob, unable to decide, every second stretching out like a held note that won't end.

Carlos had promised himself he would not be the kind of father who waited up, and yet here he was at one in the morning, sitting on the bottom stair in the dark. It wasn't curfew that worried him. It was the call he'd gotten at eleven, a wrong number, a man breathing and then saying, very clearly, your boy owes money. Then a click. Carlos had told himself it was a prank. He had told himself that Luis was a good kid, a straight-A kid, that he didn't gamble or deal or anything like that. But then he'd gone through Luis's room and found the envelope taped under the drawer, the cash, more than Carlos made in a month. Now every car that passed slowly made his whole body tense. When one stopped across the street with its engine running, he crept to the window and peered through the blinds, his heart hammering against his ribs so hard his shirt seemed to move. He slid his hand toward the cordless phone and held it, thumb on the nine, waiting.

Agnieszka had never minded being alone in the house at night until tonight. Her husband was away for work, and their son Pawel had gone out with friends, and now it was half past twelve and there was a sound coming from the garage. A scrape. A soft thump. Pawel had his own key and always came in through the front door, always, slamming it so hard the pictures rattled. This was different. Slow. Careful. Agnieszka sat bolt upright on the couch, the television muted, her ears straining. Another thump. She texted her son with clumsy thumbs: are you home? No reply. She stood and her knees were trembling. She picked up the heavy flashlight from the kitchen drawer and crept toward the door to the garage, every board in the floor creaking under her, and stopped with her hand an inch from the knob. Her breath was coming quick and shallow through her mouth. On the other side, something shifted against the door. She did not open it. She backed away until she hit the counter, eyes locked on the handle.

The email from the manager just said: Can you come see me? Now, please. No smiley face, which Nkechi's manager always used, even when announcing layoffs. Especially then. Nkechi read it at her desk and felt her stomach plunge. Three people had been walked out last week carrying boxes. She had the mortgage, the twins' daycare, and her mother's medication, all on her single paycheck. She stood up and her chair rolled back and bumped the filing cabinet loudly, and two people glanced over. Walking down the hall, she felt as if the corridor was getting longer. She smoothed her blouse and her palms left damp marks on the fabric. Outside the office door she paused, hearing low voices inside, a second voice she did not recognize. HR? Her mouth went so dry she had to swallow three times before she could knock. When the door opened and she saw the woman from human resources sitting there with a thin folder, her ears started to ring, and she lowered herself into the chair without being asked because she wasn't sure she could stay upright.

My manager closed the door behind me, and then he locked it. I heard the little click and something in my spine went cold. Mr. Fairbanks has always been the type to stand too close, to put a hand on your lower back while he explains a spreadsheet, and I'd started planning my days around never being alone with him. Now the blinds were down. He sat on the edge of his desk, between me and the door, and said he'd been reviewing my performance and had some concerns, but maybe we could work something out. He smiled. I could hear my own heartbeat in my ears. My hands were clamped together in my lap so hard my rings dug into my fingers. I'm Delphine, I'm twenty-three, this is my first real job, and I didn't know what you're supposed to say. I said I should get back to my desk. My voice sounded like a child's. He didn't move. I stared at the doorknob behind him, measuring the distance, wondering whether he'd stop me if I stood up.

When the manager called Arjun into her office, there were two men in dark suits already sitting there, and one of them had a badge clipped to his belt. Federal. Arjun's heart lurched so hard he felt it in his throat. Two months ago he had signed off on a set of invoices his supervisor had pushed across the desk, saying it was routine, just sign here, and he had signed without reading carefully because he was tired and the supervisor was his boss. The men stood up when he came in. One of them said his name, full name, including the middle one nobody used. Arjun's knees felt watery. His tie was suddenly strangling him. He sat when told to sit, and his hands would not stay still; they kept straightening the cuffs of his shirt, then the pen on the table, then his cuffs again. The agent opened a folder and slid a photograph across, and it was his own signature, enlarged, and Arjun's vision went grey at the edges as he stared at the curve of the letters he had made.

I could tell from the way the room went silent that it was bad. Every head on the warehouse floor turned to watch me walk toward the supervisor's office, and then every head turned quickly away. That morning, a forklift had backed into a rack in aisle nine and brought down a whole pallet of floor tile, and a temp named Bryce had been underneath it. The ambulance had come. Nobody knew anything yet. And I was the one who had signed the safety inspection for that rack on Friday. I'd signed it without checking the anchor bolts because we were behind and the shift lead had been yelling. My name is Ulrich and I've worked here eight years and right then I felt like I might throw up on the concrete. My boots felt like they were full of sand. My heart was banging. I kept seeing that signature, my own initials, small and neat on the clipboard, and the pallet coming down, and Bryce's yellow vest disappearing underneath. I knocked, and my knuckles barely made a sound.

The night manager at the hotel, Mrs. Castellano, asked Thandiwe to come to the back office at the end of her shift, and to bring her passport. Thandiwe's hands stopped moving on the towels she was folding. Her passport. The one with the visa that had run out in March. The one she had shown no one since. She finished the stack slowly, very slowly, her fingers clumsy on the corners. Her pulse was jumping in her neck. She thought about her son at home with the neighbor, about the rent paid up only until Friday, about the room in the detention center that a cousin had described, the bright lights that never turned off. When she walked to the office she kept her eyes down, and every footstep echoing in the empty hallway sounded like it belonged to somebody following her. She stopped outside the door and could not make her hand lift to knock. Inside, she heard Mrs. Castellano on the phone, saying yes, she is here, yes, I will keep her until you arrive.

Elias was the youngest engineer on the bridge project, and the email from his manager came at 4:58 on a Friday with the subject line: Your load calculations. Please come now. He had run those numbers three times. Hadn't he? Walking down the hall, he went through it in his head and found the gap he had been avoiding all week: he'd used the old wind data, the 2009 tables, because the new ones were still in draft. The bridge had opened to traffic Monday. Thousands of cars crossed it every day. School buses crossed it. A wave of heat climbed up his neck and then drained away and left him cold and clammy. In the office his manager had the drawings spread on the table and her face was grey. She didn't say hello. She just pointed at a single figure circled in red and asked him where it came from. Elias opened his mouth and his voice had gone hoarse. His eyes went to the window, to the long span visible in the distance, and to the cars on it, small and steady and trusting.

Wedged behind a loose board in the attic, Gwendolyn found an envelope addressed to her mother in handwriting she did not recognize. The postmark was from 1984. Inside was a single page. I know what you did to that girl, and I will not stay quiet forever. Underneath was a newspaper clipping about a teenager who had gone missing from the next town that summer and was never found. Gwendolyn's mother had been nineteen then. Gwendolyn sat back on her heels in the dust, the paper suddenly heavy in her hands. A chill ran over her scalp and down her arms. Her mother was downstairs right now, making tea, humming. Gwendolyn listened to the humming through the floorboards and felt her breath go shallow and quiet, as if she needed to hide the sound of it. When the stairs creaked and her mother called up asking whether she wanted honey, Gwendolyn jerked so violently that she knocked a box over, and she scrambled to shove the letter inside her sweater before the footsteps reached the top.

The letter was dated last month. That was the thing. I'd been expecting old stuff up there, my grandfather's war papers and Christmas cards from people long dead, and instead there was a crisp white envelope tucked inside a box of my baby clothes, with no stamp, no postmark, and my name written across it in neat block capitals. Nobody else has a key to this house. I moved in after my father died, and I changed the locks, and I live alone. Inside, one line: I come up here when you're asleep. My whole body went rigid. I could hear the blood rushing in my ears. I looked around the attic, at the shadows behind the chimney, at the dark gap under the eaves, the little door to the crawlspace that I'd never opened. The flashlight shook in my hand so the beam jittered across the beams. I backed toward the ladder without taking my eyes off that small door, my bare feet feeling for each rung, and when I reached the bottom I slammed the hatch shut and leaned against it, panting.

Bashir was clearing the attic so the house could go on the market when he found the letter from the county health department, addressed to the previous owners, dated 1979. It was short. Following our soil tests, we strongly recommend that you do not grow food on the property or allow children to play in the backyard. Contamination levels significantly exceed. He stopped reading there and read it again. His daughters had been playing in that backyard for six years. Making mud pies. Digging for worms. Last spring they had grown tomatoes and eaten them warm off the vine. Bashir felt heat rush into his face and then a cold sweat bloom across his back. He thought of Laila's headaches, the ones the pediatrician said were probably screen time. He thought of the rash on Samira's hands. He sat down hard on an old trunk, the letter crumpling in his fist, and found that he was struggling to pull in a full breath, as if the attic air itself had turned poisonous around him.

The letter was in my grandmother's handwriting, unmistakable, the loops on her capital letters. It was addressed to me, which was impossible, because I was born four years after she died. My dearest Zofia, it began, and my legs folded under me and I sat down on the dusty floorboards. If you are reading this, then you have the same dreams I did. You see the man at the foot of the bed. Do not speak to him. Whatever he asks, do not answer. I hadn't told anyone about the dreams. Not my mother, not my therapist, not anyone. The tall figure who stands there, silent, every night since I turned thirty. I could hear my breath sawing in and out. The attic light flickered and I gasped out loud. My fingers had gone so numb I could barely hold the page. I read the rest of it twice, faster each time, then shoved it back into the envelope and clutched it against my stomach, and I was dreading the night coming, dreading the bed, dreading closing my eyes.

Maximilian was eighty, and he knew that letter the moment he saw it in the shoebox: the thin blue airmail paper, the stamp with the old eagle. He had hidden it there himself in 1962, and he had told himself he had burned it. It was from his brother, still in the East, begging him not to report what he had seen at the border crossing, because if Max told the Americans, they would know where the information came from, and they would come for the family. Max had told them anyway. A month later the letters from his brother stopped. Now, sixty years on, his granddaughter was sorting the attic and had set the box aside with a cheerful note: Opa, looks like old mail, want to go through it together? His heart had begun stumbling in his chest. His hands shook as he unfolded the paper. He could not let her read it. He could not let anyone read it. He sat on the edge of the attic stairs, breathing in short ragged pulls, while below he heard her coming back up.

Clearing the attic was supposed to take an afternoon. Then Tamsin found the bundle of letters tied with red string under the insulation, all addressed to the house, all unopened, from a law firm in the city. She slit the top one with her thumbnail. It said the property had been seized in a judgment years ago and that the occupants were trespassing. The most recent letter was from three weeks ago, and it said, in bold type, that removal would proceed on the first of the month. That was Monday. Tamsin's heart began to thud. She had bought this house from a man who had said nothing about any judgment, paid cash, every cent of her divorce settlement. Her whole life was in this house. Her knees ached from kneeling on the joists but she did not get up. She kept tearing open envelopes, one after another, faster and faster, scanning for the words that would make it not true, her breath short and shallow in the stale hot air, sweat stinging her eyes.

Halfway through the risotto Yolanda remembered the peanut oil. She had used it in the dressing, a generous pour, without thinking, and her sister's new fiance, Bram, was coming tonight, and her sister had told her twice that his allergy was the serious kind, the ambulance kind. The salad was already tossed. It was sitting on the counter beside the bread, glistening. Yolanda stared at it and felt the wooden spoon slip from her fingers into the pot. Which bowls had touched it? Which tongs? She had used the same knife for the herbs that went into the risotto. Her heart began to slam. She grabbed the salad bowl and dumped the whole thing into the trash, then stood there with her hands hovering, not knowing what to wash first, what was safe, what was not. The doorbell rang. She jumped so hard that she knocked the pepper grinder off the counter. Through the frosted glass she could see two shapes, and she pressed her back against the refrigerator, breathing hard, her mind racing over every surface in the room.

The pan caught at 6:52. The guests were due at seven. I had turned for one second to grab the wine glasses, and when I turned back there was a sheet of flame climbing out of the skillet toward the cabinets, bright orange and roaring, and the smoke alarm began to shriek. My whole body went stiff. Every bit of advice I had ever heard evaporated from my head. Water? No. Never water. Flour? Baking soda? Where was the baking soda? My hands moved without me, yanking open drawers, flinging dish towels aside. The flames licked the underside of the cabinet and I heard the paint start to blister and pop. I'm Callum, I'm thirty-one, I'd been so pleased with myself for hosting, and now I couldn't remember where the fire extinguisher was in my own flat. My eyes stung. My throat was raw from the smoke. I finally found the lid and slammed it down over the pan, and stood there holding it with both hands, coughing, shaking, watching the scorched cabinet above me for any glint of orange.

Mei-Ling's mother-in-law had never once eaten a meal Mei-Ling cooked without finding something wrong with it. And tonight was the night her husband's whole family was coming, all eleven of them, to decide, unofficially but really, whether she was a suitable wife. That was how it felt anyway. The dumplings were splitting in the steamer. The soup was too salty; she tasted it again and her tongue curled. The fish, which was supposed to be the centerpiece, had come out of the oven dry at the edges. Her heart was pounding so loudly she could hear it over the extractor fan. She kept wiping her hands on her apron even though they were already clean. The last time, her mother-in-law had made a comment in front of everyone, and her husband had laughed along, and Mei-Ling had cried in the bathroom for twenty minutes. A car door slammed in the driveway. Then another, and another. Mei-Ling froze with a pair of chopsticks halfway to a dumpling, and her stomach cramped so tightly she had to lean forward against the counter.

Chef Ambrose had cooked for presidents, but the man coming to his restaurant tonight was the one who had threatened to break his fingers. The message had come through his maître d' at lunch: Mr. Volkov and four guests, eight o'clock, the private room, and he expects the chef to serve personally. Ambrose owed Volkov money from the renovation, a great deal of it, and had missed two payments. Now he stood in his kitchen, slicing shallots with a knife that kept slipping on the board, and he could not stop looking at his hands. The left one was shaking. He had never in thirty years of cooking had a shaking hand. His sous-chef asked if he was all right and he snapped at her, his voice coming out cracked and high. He could feel sweat soaking through the back of his whites. He plated the first course with exaggerated care, wiping every drip, every smear, as if perfection could buy him something. When he heard the front door and voices he did not know, he put the knife down and gripped the steel counter.

I didn't recognize the mushrooms. That's the stupid thing. My neighbor gave me a basket of them from the woods behind his place, and I sauteed them in butter with thyme, and I'd already eaten a forkful while tasting the sauce, and then I looked up chanterelles on my phone and the pictures didn't quite match. The ridges were wrong. The color was wrong. There was another one, a lookalike, with a name I couldn't pronounce and a list of symptoms that started six hours after ingestion and ended with liver failure. My stomach clenched. Was that real, or was I imagining it? My guests, eight of them, were due in fifteen minutes. The pan was still steaming on the stove. I scraped the whole thing into the bin, then fished one out with my fingers to photograph it, my hand trembling so badly the picture blurred. I'm Rhiannon. I'm a careful person. I called poison control and while the line rang I stood at the sink, staring at my own reflection in the dark window, feeling for any cramp.

Fourteen-year-old Ezra was cooking dinner because his mom was in the bedroom with the door shut again, and his dad's truck was going to pull into the driveway at six. When dinner wasn't ready on time, things got thrown. Last week it was a plate, and the week before that it was his mom's phone, against the wall, right next to her head. It was 5:48. The rice was still crunchy. The chicken was pink in the middle when Ezra cut into it, and his hands began to shake so badly that the knife clattered onto the cutting board. He turned the heat up as high as it would go. He set the table, three plates, forks on the left, exactly the way his dad liked, and straightened the napkins twice. He kept glancing at the clock on the microwave. 5:53. His stomach felt hollow and sick. When he heard the rumble of the engine turning onto their street, he stood perfectly still in the middle of the kitchen, holding a wooden spoon, his ears straining for the sound of the truck door.

The movers had left by eight, and Juniper sat on a box in the middle of her new apartment in a city where she knew no one, listening to the building. It was louder than she had expected. Someone upstairs was dragging furniture. Someone in the hallway was shouting into a phone in a language she did not speak. Then, very close, right outside her door, she heard footsteps stop. She waited for a knock. There wasn't one. The footsteps just stopped, and stayed, and she could see the shadow of two feet under the gap. Her breath caught. She had not yet changed the locks; the landlord had said the previous tenant left on bad terms and had never returned his key. Juniper stood up very slowly, the box creaking under her, and tiptoed to the kitchen, where she pulled a knife from the block she had only just unpacked. She stood holding it in front of her with both hands, the tip wavering, eyes fixed on the shadow, her heart going so hard her vision pulsed with it.

Nobody told me the apartment was above a bar. I found out on the first night, at one in the morning, when the floor started vibrating with bass and then a fight spilled out onto the sidewalk below my window. Glass breaking. Someone screaming. I'm Abebe, I'm from a small town where my family's door was never locked, and I had moved here for a job I'd wanted for years, and suddenly I was lying on a bare mattress on the floor with my heart going like a drum. I could hear a man's voice shouting threats, and then the scrape of something metal on the pavement. I crawled to the window and peeked through the edge of the blinds and saw blood on the curb. I ducked back down and pressed my spine flat against the wall. My hands were cold. I counted my money in my head, my savings, the deposit I'd already paid, the lease I'd signed for twelve months. Twelve months. When the sirens came I didn't move. I sat there clutching my knees until the sky turned pale.

Imogen found the first sign on the second day: a stain on the bathroom ceiling, faint, the shape of a hand. She scrubbed it. By evening it was back, darker. On the third night she woke at 3:14 to the sound of water running, and when she went to the bathroom the faucet was on full, though she knew she had turned it off. Her skin crawled. She told herself it was old plumbing, an old building. She was a rational woman, a statistician. But when she mentioned it to the building superintendent, a gruff Albanian named Driton, he went quiet and asked which unit, and then said, very carefully, that the last tenant had not stayed long either. Now it was night again. Imogen sat up in bed with every light in the apartment on and her laptop open, pretending to work. Every few seconds her eyes flicked toward the bathroom door. Her mouth was dry. She had pushed a chair against it, which was absurd, and she knew it was absurd, and she checked that it was still there anyway.

My new apartment is on the nineteenth floor, which seemed thrilling when I signed the lease and seems like a terrible mistake now that I'm standing on the balcony. I have always had a thing about heights. Not a phobia, I'd tell people, just a thing. The railing is waist high, glass, and through it I can see everything, all the way down, the cars as small as beetles. The wind pushes at my back. My knees go loose and I grab the door frame so hard it hurts. I step back inside and my heart is racing, my palms are wet, and there's a ringing in my ears that won't stop. I came to this city to start over after the breakup, and the realtor kept saying the view, the view, and I kept nodding, and I never once went out onto the balcony during the tour. I slide the door shut and lock it and draw the curtain, and then I stand in the living room with my back pressed to the opposite wall, as far from the glass as I can get. My name is Pernille. I have a year's lease.

Jae-won had moved halfway across the country to get away from his ex, and he had told nobody the address. Not his old coworkers, not his old friends, only his sister and the post office. So on the first morning in the new apartment, when he opened the door to go buy coffee and found a bouquet of white lilies on the mat, the same kind his ex used to send after every fight, every apology, he went completely still. There was no card. There didn't need to be one. He felt the blood drain from his face. His fingers on the doorknob turned to ice. He looked up and down the hallway, which was empty, and at the stairwell door, which was swinging gently closed. He slammed his own door and threw the deadbolt and the chain, and then he backed into the middle of the empty living room, among his unopened boxes, breathing fast and shallow. He fumbled out his phone and called his sister and when she answered he couldn't get a single word out, only her name, over and over.

The landlord had said the neighborhood was improving, and Florence, who was sixty-eight and had never lived anywhere but the village in Devon, believed him because she wanted to. Her daughter lived three streets over. That had been the whole point. But on her first evening, walking back from the shops, three young men fell into step behind her. Not close. Just there. She sped up, and they sped up. She turned a corner, and they turned it too. Her shopping bag was cutting into her fingers and her breath was coming in little puffs she couldn't control. She didn't know which streets led where. She didn't know which doors were safe to knock on. Her heart was jumping erratically, the way it did before the doctor changed her tablets. She clutched her handbag against her chest with her free arm. When she finally saw her own building, she half ran the last stretch, fumbling with the unfamiliar keys, dropping them, snatching them up off the pavement, and only when the heavy door swung shut behind her did she dare to turn around.

At mile twenty-five Leopold's chest started doing something it had never done before. Not the usual burn of a long run, but a squeezing, deep in the middle, like a fist closing. He slowed. The fist did not let go. A strange numbness tingled down his left arm into his fingers. He was fifty-six and his doctor had cleared him, but his father had died at fifty-eight shoveling snow, and the thought arrived uninvited and lodged itself in his skull. The crowd along the barriers was cheering, waving signs, ringing cowbells, and the noise seemed suddenly far away, as if he were underwater. Sweat that felt cold instead of hot was running into his eyes. He wanted to stop but stopping felt dangerous too, like if he stopped he might fall. His breath came short and shallow. He searched the sidelines for a medical tent, for anyone in a red cross vest, and his eyes kept jumping from face to face without landing anywhere, and the finish line, a mile away, looked impossibly far.

I was in the last mile when I heard it: a sharp crack, then another, from somewhere up ahead near the finish. Not fireworks. The crowd went silent for one second, and then everyone was screaming. People were climbing over the barriers, shoving, running in every direction. A woman ran straight past me against the course, her race bib flapping, her face twisted. I stopped dead in the road. My legs, which had been burning, suddenly went light and shaky in a completely different way. My husband and our two kids had been waiting at the finish line. They'd had a sign. I'd been looking forward to seeing it for twenty-five miles. I'm Esperanza, I'm a schoolteacher, and in that moment I couldn't think, couldn't move, my heart pounding so hard my vision jolted with every beat. Then I ran. Toward it. I pushed past people coming the other way, sobbing their names, my voice shredded and hoarse, scanning the faces, my lungs tearing, every part of me braced for what I might see.

Kalinda's vision started to go strange around mile twenty-five and a half. The edges of everything shimmered, and the road seemed to tilt a little to the right, though she knew it was flat. She'd skipped the last water station because she was on pace for a qualifying time. Now her hands were tingling and her lips felt numb and her thoughts were coming slowly, like syrup. She had read about hyponatremia, about runners who collapsed and seized and never woke up. Or was it the other thing, dehydration? She couldn't remember which one this was. She couldn't remember which one you treated with water. That blankness was the worst part, reaching for a thought and finding nothing there. She staggered and caught herself. A spectator called out that she was almost there, and his voice warbled strangely. Kalinda's heart was racing much faster than her pace should allow. She kept running because she didn't know what else to do, but she kept one hand stretched out toward the barrier beside her, ready to grab it.

The thunder rolled in at mile twenty-five, and then the sky above the bay went the color of a bruise. The officials hadn't stopped the race. I'm Oswaldo, I've run eleven marathons, and I've never seen lightning like that, jagged white cracks dropping straight into the water a few hundred yards away, close enough that I heard a hiss before the boom. The hair on my arms rose. Every runner around me picked up the pace without a word. The course here runs along the seawall, totally exposed, nothing taller than us for half a mile in any direction. My wet shirt clung to me and I felt like a lightning rod, like a target. My breath was ragged, not from the running but from something tighter, higher in my chest. Another strike, closer. Someone ahead of me threw herself flat on the pavement. I didn't know if I should do that too. I kept running, crouched low, my head ducked down between my shoulders, counting the seconds between flash and sound and watching the number shrink.

Rosamund's knee had been aching since mile eighteen, but at mile twenty-five it made a sound, a wet pop she felt more than heard, and then it buckled. She caught herself on her hands. The asphalt scraped her palms raw. When she tried to straighten the leg, a hot, enormous pain shot up her thigh and she cried out. She knew that pop. She'd heard her teammate describe it in college, the year he tore his ACL and never ran competitively again. Running was the only thing that had held her together after her husband's death. It was the only reason she left the house most days. Lying on the course with other runners swerving around her, she felt a cold dread spread through her stomach that had nothing to do with the pain. What would she be without this? She pressed her hands against the asphalt and tried to push up and her whole body shook. A volunteer in a yellow vest jogged toward her, and Rosamund heard herself saying no, no, I'm fine, over and over, in a voice gone high and thin.

With one mile left, Tariq realized the man in the blue windbreaker had been running beside him for too long. Not racing. Not wearing a bib. Just keeping pace, a little behind his shoulder, matching every change of speed. Tariq had testified in a trial last month. The defendant's brother had looked at him across the courtroom the whole time, a flat, steady look, and his lawyer had told him to be careful for a while. Now the hair on the back of Tariq's neck stood up. He sped up. The man sped up. He slowed. So did the man. His heart, already working hard, began to pound in a ragged, uneven way. He couldn't see a police officer anywhere, only cheering strangers holding signs. His mouth went sour. He drifted toward the edge of the course, close to the crowd, as if they could shield him, and he kept glancing sideways, trying to see the man's hands, trying to see whether he was holding anything, and his own legs suddenly felt clumsy and weak, like they might fold under him.

Buster always came back when Wilhelmina rattled the treat jar. Always. It was the one trick he had never failed in eleven years. She rattled it again on the back step, harder, and the sound went out into the dark yard and nothing came back. Not a jingle of tags. Not a bark. Just the wind in the cedar hedge. Her chest tightened. She had heard coyotes the night before, yipping close, closer than ever, and she'd told herself the fence was high enough. She stepped down into the cold grass in her slippers, sweeping the flashlight beam left and right. The beam shook. She called his name, and her voice cracked in the middle of it. At the far corner of the yard, near the back gate, the beam caught something on the ground: tufts of pale fur, scattered, and a dark smear on the fence post. Wilhelmina's breath stopped. The flashlight slipped in her wet palm. She stood rooted to the spot, mouth open, unable to make herself walk the last ten feet.

I let Pepper out for five minutes while I unloaded groceries. Five minutes. When I went back to the door, the gate was standing open and the yard was empty, and the street beyond it is a four-lane road where people do fifty in a thirty. I was down the driveway before I knew I was moving. Cars whipped past one after another, headlights glaring, and my heart was in my throat because I kept seeing shapes in the road that turned out to be leaves, a bag, a shadow. I'm Benedikt and I'm a grown man, a firefighter, and my legs were shaking so badly I had to put a hand on the mailbox. I screamed her name across the traffic. A truck blared its horn at me as I stepped off the curb, and I jumped back with a jolt that went down to my toes. I started running along the shoulder, calling and calling, my voice going hoarse, and every time I heard brakes squeal anywhere in the neighborhood my whole body went cold.

The neighbor's warning had been taped to Ottoline's mailbox that morning. Someone was putting out poisoned meat in the neighborhood; two cats on Elm Street had already died. She'd read it and thought, well, Rufus is a dog, and he stays in the yard. Now Rufus had been out for forty minutes, and he had not come when called, and when she finally found him behind the woodpile he was lying on his side, panting fast and shallow, with foam at the corners of his mouth. Ottoline dropped to her knees on the frozen dirt. His eyes rolled toward her but did not focus. Her hands hovered over him, not knowing where to touch. She could not breathe properly. Was it the poison? How long ago? Was there time? She scooped him up, all forty pounds of him, and staggered toward the car, his head lolling against her arm, and her own heart was beating so fast and hard it hurt. She fumbled the keys twice. Her voice kept saying his name, high and strange, as if from somebody else's mouth.

It was only after Aleksander had called for Bruno for ten minutes that he noticed the hole under the fence, freshly dug, the dirt still dark. Beyond the fence was the old quarry, a hundred feet of sheer drop into black water, with signs every few yards warning people to stay back. Bruno was half blind now, an old dog who bumped into furniture. Aleksander squeezed through the gap in the boards, tearing his jacket on a nail, and stumbled through the dry brush toward the rim. His breath was coming in gasps. The night was moonless and the beam of his phone flashlight only reached a few feet. He called the dog's name and it echoed back off the quarry walls, empty and hollow. He crept forward until the ground under his feet started to slope, and he dropped onto his hands and knees and crawled the last stretch, gripping roots, his heart lurching, and shone the light down over the edge into nothing, the beam disappearing into the dark long before it reached the water.
