The storm was coming fast, the sky turning a weird greenish yellow, and the tornado sirens had just started their long rising wail, and Daisy was not inside. Twelve-year-old Mackenzie stood at the back door yelling for her in a voice that kept breaking. The wind was already bending the trees sideways. Her mom was yelling from the basement stairs to get down here now, right now. Mackenzie couldn't make herself leave the door. Daisy hid under the deck whenever it thundered; she might be under there right now, shaking. Mackenzie took one step out onto the porch and the wind nearly yanked the screen door off its hinges. Something, a branch or a lawn chair, went flying across the yard. Her heart was thumping so hard it made her dizzy. She dropped to her stomach on the porch boards and peered through the slats, calling, crying, her fingers hooked in the gaps, while behind her, her mother's voice rose to a shriek.

Cosmo didn't come back in after his last trip outside, and Jarrah went out to the yard to find him standing rigid by the back hedge, hackles raised, growling at something in the dark. Cosmo never growled. He was a soft, silly retriever who loved the mailman. Jarrah stopped walking. The growl went on, low and steady, and the dog's whole body was pointed at the black gap between the hedge and the shed. There was a smell, too, musky and rank, that hadn't been there before. Jarrah's skin prickled from his scalp to his heels. They lived on the edge of the national park, and last week the rangers had put up a notice about a bear. He whispered the dog's name. Cosmo did not turn. Something moved in the shadow, something big, and a twig snapped with a sound like a gunshot. Jarrah's legs went weak. He reached out very slowly and grabbed Cosmo's collar and began backing toward the house, step by step, never looking away, his breath stuck halfway down his throat.

From the wings Anouk could see the hall filling, all two thousand seats, the murmur rising like the sound of the sea. Her hands were ice. She pressed them under her armpits but they would not warm. She was going to play the Rachmaninoff, and in rehearsal yesterday her memory had gone completely white in the middle of the second movement for three full bars, and she had sat with her fingers hovering over the keys while the conductor stared at her. It had never happened before. Now she could not stop thinking about it. What if it came back? What if it came back in front of all of them, and the critics, and her old teacher in the fifth row? Her stomach was churning so violently she had already been sick once in the dressing room. Her heart fluttered against her ribs. The stage manager touched her elbow and said one minute, and Anouk nodded, and swallowed, and found that she could not make her feet move toward the light.

Fifteen minutes before our set, the club owner came backstage and said there was a guy in the crowd asking for me by name. Big guy, tattoos, said he was my old bandmate's brother. My old bandmate is dead. He overdosed in a van three years ago, on tour with us, and his family blamed me for it because I was the one who brought the stuff on board. I'd never met the brother, but I'd read his messages. Every one of them. I'm Fitzgerald, I play bass, and I was suddenly sitting on an amp case with my head between my knees trying to breathe. My hands were tingling. I could hear the crowd through the wall, the drunk laughter, the clink of bottles, and somewhere in there, him. Our drummer said we could cancel. I said no. Then I said maybe. When the lights went down and the intro tape started, I picked up my bass with fingers that wouldn't close properly around the neck, and I walked out with my eyes on the floor so I wouldn't have to see his face.

Valentina was seven and this was her first recital, and she had been excited all week until she peeked through the curtain and saw the rows and rows of grown-ups. Now she stood backstage holding her tiny violin by the neck, her bow arm stiff as a stick. Her tummy hurt. Her knees were wobbling under the stiff skirt of her new dress. Every time someone in the audience coughed, she flinched. The boy who went before her had cried in the middle of his song and everyone had gone quiet and then some of the big kids had laughed, and she had watched his face turn red and crumple. What if that happened to her? What if she forgot the song? Her eyes kept filling up and she kept blinking them clear. When her teacher bent down and whispered that it was her turn, Valentina grabbed a fistful of her teacher's sleeve and would not let go, shaking her head hard, her mouth pressed into a thin wobbling line, her breath coming out in little hitches.

I'm standing at the side of the stage at the festival and I can't stop looking at the lighting rig. Forty minutes ago, during soundcheck, a clamp on the truss above the drum riser gave way and a can light swung down on its safety cable, missing our drummer's head by maybe a foot. The crew said they fixed it. They said it's all good, mate, all tightened up. But the wind has picked up since then, and the whole structure is groaning, swaying a little, I swear it's swaying. I'm Siddharth, I sing, and in four minutes I'm supposed to stand directly under that thing in front of twenty thousand people. My throat has closed so tight I'm not sure I could sing if I wanted to. My palms are slick on the mic. Each gust of wind makes the steel creak, and I hear it over the crowd, over everything. When the stage manager waves us on, my legs carry me forward but my eyes stay up, on the rig, on every bolt, waiting for one of them to move.

Bertrand had played the cello in the orchestra for thirty-one years without ever once thinking about his hands. Then, last month, the trembling had started. A fine tremor in the left one, there at rest, gone when he reached for something, and his neurologist had used a long name and asked him to come back in six weeks. Tonight was the Elgar, the solo, the one he had practiced since he was a boy. Backstage he held his left hand flat in front of him and watched it. It was shaking. Just slightly. Just enough. His chest was tight and every breath seemed to stop halfway. What if it showed in the vibrato? What if the whole hall heard it, his colleagues, his wife in the box, and knew? He clenched the hand into a fist and released it, clenched and released. Sweat beaded at his hairline under the stage lights' glow from the wings. The conductor was walking out. The applause swelled. Bertrand picked up his bow and his heart was hammering so hard he felt it in his throat.

Nobody in the village knew that Amina sang. Her father had forbidden it, called it shameful, and when he had caught her singing along to the radio at fifteen he had smashed the radio against the wall. Now she was twenty-two and living in the city and she had signed up, in a moment of madness, for the open mic at a cafe. Her name was third on the list. She sat at the back with her coat still on, buttoned up to her chin, and her teeth were chattering though the room was warm. A man by the window had a phone out, filming. What if someone posted it? What if someone from home saw? She pictured her father's face, his hand coming up, and she felt her body shrink into the chair. The second performer finished. People clapped. The host read her name off the clipboard and looked around the room, and Amina's heart pounded so hard she felt sick, and she gripped the edge of the table and did not stand, did not stand, could not.

The box on Philippa's doorstep had no return address, and her name was spelled out in letters cut from magazines, each one a different size and color. She stood on the porch with her keys still in her hand and did not touch it. She was a county judge. Last week she had sentenced a man to twenty years, and his family had shouted at her from the gallery as the bailiffs dragged him out. The box was about the size of a shoebox and wrapped very neatly in brown paper. She leaned closer without meaning to, and she thought she heard something, a faint tick, or maybe that was her own pulse thudding in her ears. Her mouth went bone dry. She took one step back, then another, very slowly, as if any sudden movement might set something off. Her heel caught the edge of the top step and she nearly fell. She fumbled her phone out with numb fingers and walked backward all the way to the sidewalk, never turning around, before she dialed.

Inside the package was my own diary. The one I kept at sixteen, the pink one with the broken lock, the one I lost when we moved out of the house on Fairview twenty years ago. I'm Henrietta, I'm thirty-six now, and I stood at the kitchen counter holding it while the blood drained from my hands. There was no note. Just the diary, and when I flipped through it with trembling fingers I saw that someone had written in it. In the margins. In red pen, in a small, careful hand. Next to the entry about my first kiss: I watched. Next to the entry about the night my parents fought: I was outside the window. Page after page. My breath got shorter and shorter. The kitchen felt huge and exposed, with the big window over the sink showing the dark backyard. I yanked the blind down so hard it came off one bracket and dangled. Then I stood in the corner by the fridge, the diary clutched against my chest, listening to every sound the house made.

The package for Dimitri was addressed in his own handwriting. He knew it immediately; nobody else made a capital D with that strange double loop. But he hadn't sent it. He was sure of that. He had no memory of the box, of the tape, of writing his address on the label in black marker, and that was the part that made his stomach drop. Since the accident last spring there had been gaps. Small ones. His car parked on a different street than he remembered. A receipt in his wallet from a hardware store he'd never been to. His doctor had called them minor episodes. Dimitri set the box down on the kitchen table and stared at it, sweat prickling along his hairline. What would he have mailed to himself? Why? He took a knife from the drawer to cut the tape, and his hand was shaking so badly that the blade skittered across the cardboard. Inside, under a layer of newspaper, was a key he did not recognize and a note in his handwriting that said: Don't trust her.

The package said it was from Fernhill Pharmaceuticals, and the box was cold to the touch, ice packs inside, and nestled in the foam was a glass vial with a handwritten label and a syringe. The letter, on company letterhead, thanked Priscilla for enrolling in the trial and reminded her to administer the first dose tonight. She had never enrolled in any trial. She had never heard of Fernhill. Her fingers went cold, colder than the ice packs. She read the letter again and saw her full name, her date of birth, her insurance number, and the name of her own physician, Dr. Mwangi, listed as the referring doctor. How did they have all of this? She put the vial down on the counter very carefully, as if it might shatter just from being looked at. Her heart was beating fast and light like a bird's. She looked at the syringe and thought of the people who would have just done what the letter said, and the hair on her arms stood up, and she backed away from the counter, wiping her hands on her jeans.

There was a smell coming from the box. Faint, sweetish, wrong. I noticed it as soon as I carried it in from the step, before I'd even looked at the label, and I put it on the hall table and stared at it. Brown cardboard, damp at one corner, a darker stain spreading slowly through the bottom edge. No sender. Just my name, Lorcan, and this address. My skin went tight all over. Two weeks ago I'd reported my business partner to the authorities for what he was doing with the company accounts, and he had found out who it was within a day, and he'd left me a voicemail I still hadn't deleted, very quiet, very even, telling me I'd regret it. My pulse was beating in my temples. I didn't want to open it. I didn't want to not open it. I stood in the hallway with my back against the front door, eyes on that slowly spreading stain, my breath shallow, and the smell crept toward me, and I couldn't make my hand reach for the phone.

Esther's package came from the Department of Immigration, which was strange, because the department did not send packages. They sent letters. The box was heavy for its size. Inside, wrapped in plastic, were her own documents: her original birth certificate from Kampala, her marriage certificate, the old passport, all the papers she had submitted with her application three years ago. Returned. On top was a form with a single box ticked, and the word under it began with WITHDR, and she stopped reading there. Her hands went numb. The kitchen around her seemed to recede, the hum of the refrigerator getting louder and louder until it was the only sound in the world. Her children were at school. Her husband was at the plant. They had built everything here on the assumption that this application would work. She sat down on the floor because there was no chair close enough, the papers spilling across her lap, and her breath came in tight little gasps, and she kept turning the form over and over as if the back might say something else.

Clementine and her brother Rafael were halfway through Grandma's bedroom closet when Rafael pulled down the hatbox and went pale. Inside were dozens of envelopes, all addressed to their grandmother, all from the same prison in Texas, spanning forty years. The most recent was postmarked three weeks before she died. Clementine took one with fingers that suddenly felt clumsy. It was signed by a man with their surname. Their grandfather. Who, they had always been told, had died in a car crash in 1979. The letter said: When I get out, I'm coming for what's mine. Clementine looked at the date on the envelope, then at her brother. Rafael was already searching his phone, his thumbs jerky, and when he looked up his face had gone grey. The man's release date had been last Tuesday. Clementine felt the room shrink around her. She looked toward the window, at the street, at the strange car that had been parked across from the house since they arrived that morning, and her stomach lurched so hard she had to sit on the bed.

My sister found the pill organizer in Nana's nightstand and held it up and said, these are all still full. All of them. Weeks of them. Morning, noon, night, every little compartment still loaded. I didn't understand at first, and then I did, and my mouth went dry. Nana was supposed to be taking those. Her heart pills. The hospital had said it was sudden, a failure in her sleep, at eighty-four nobody asks many questions. But the organizer was full. And the home aide, Marcy, the one who had been so sweet, who had told us not to worry, Nana's doing great, the one Nana changed her will for in the spring. I felt cold crawl up the back of my neck. My sister Keturah and I looked at each other without speaking. Out in the hall, the front door opened. Marcy's voice called out cheerfully that she'd brought boxes to help us pack. Keturah shoved the pill case into her coat pocket so fast she ripped the seam, and I stood there with my heart slamming, trying to arrange my face.

Lorenzo had always been the brave one, the older brother, but when they pried open the locked cabinet in their grandmother's basement he took a step back and grabbed Giulia's arm. Rows of glass jars lined the shelves, each labeled in their grandmother's spidery handwriting with a name and a date. Some of the names they knew: the neighbor who had died suddenly in 1991, the man from church, their own grandfather. Inside the jars were locks of hair, fingernail clippings, a tooth. Giulia's breath came out in a thin whistle. The single bulb overhead buzzed and flickered. At the end of the shelf, the last jar was empty, and the label had two names on it, and they were theirs. Lorenzo's hand tightened on his sister's arm until it hurt. Neither of them moved. Somewhere upstairs, in the house that was supposed to be empty, a floorboard creaked, then another, slow and deliberate, crossing the kitchen right above their heads. Giulia pressed both hands over her mouth to keep from making a sound.

We were sorting Oma's jewelry when my brother Joost found the letter from the bank tucked inside the velvet lining. It said that a second mortgage had been taken out on the house in 2019 and that payments had stopped eight months ago. The house was supposed to be our inheritance. More than that, it was where I lived. I had moved in to take care of her, and I had given up my apartment, and every cent I had went into her medical bills. Now Joost was reading the numbers out loud, and with each one my chest got tighter, as if he were stacking bricks on it. Foreclosure proceedings. Thirty days to vacate. I'm Mirjam, forty-nine, and I haven't worked full time in six years. I sat down heavily on Oma's bed, the springs groaning, and the jewelry slid off my lap and scattered across the floor. My hands had started trembling and I sat on them to make them stop. Joost was saying something about lawyers, about options, and I couldn't hear him over the rushing in my ears.

In the bottom drawer of their grandmother's desk, under the tax returns, Callista and her younger brother Dominic, whom everyone called Dom, found the medical file. Genetic screening, 1998. Their grandmother had tested positive for a mutation, and in the margin, in her neat schoolteacher's handwriting, she had written: Passed to Elaine? Must tell the children. Elaine was their mother. Their mother had died at forty-one, of the same cancer, and nobody had ever said anything about genes. Callista was thirty-nine. She read the paragraph twice and her heart started knocking against her ribs. She thought of the lump she'd felt in the shower two weeks ago and decided was nothing. She looked over at Dom, who was twenty-eight and had a newborn daughter, and saw him doing the same arithmetic, his lips moving silently. Neither of them spoke. The house was very quiet. The old clock on the mantel ticked, and Callista realized she was holding her breath, and her fingers had gone white around the edges of the folder.

The attic stairs in Grandmother Hyacinth's house were steep and rotten, and Lucinda had told her older brother Wendell not to go up alone. He went anyway, to get the trunk of old photographs, and she was in the kitchen wrapping teacups when she heard the crack, then the crash, then nothing at all. She ran. Wendell lay at the bottom of the attic stairs in a tangle, a broken step beside him, one leg bent at a horrible angle. He wasn't moving. Lucinda dropped to her knees beside him and her hands fluttered over him, not knowing where it was safe to touch. His eyes were closed. She put her ear to his mouth and couldn't tell if the faint breath she felt was his or her own. She said his name, and then screamed it. Her phone was in the kitchen. She did not want to leave him. Her whole body was shaking so violently her teeth clacked together. She scrambled up and ran for the phone, slipping on the hallway runner, sobbing, then ran back again before she had even dialed.

The glass of the front door was spiderwebbed, and Mr. Adeyemi's key stopped halfway to the lock. Someone had broken in over the weekend. The question, the one that froze him on the sidewalk with the key in his hand, was whether they were still inside. He could see through the cracked glass into the dim shop: the register drawer hanging open, shelves knocked over, a single light on in the back storeroom that he had definitely turned off on Saturday. Then a shadow passed across that light. His heart gave a huge, painful kick. He took one step back, then another, out to the curb. His fingers were numb. He tried to call the police and his thumb kept missing the numbers. He moved behind a parked van and crouched there, peering around its bumper, his breath fast and shallow, his knees aching on the cold concrete. Every few seconds he looked back at the door, at the storeroom light, waiting for it to open, waiting for whoever it was to come out and see him.

I unlock the bakery at five every Monday, and every Monday for the past month there's been the same man waiting across the street. He doesn't come in. He just stands by the bus shelter, hood up, hands in his pockets, and watches me open. Last Monday he took a picture with his phone. Today he isn't at the bus shelter. Today, when I come around the corner from the parking lot, he's standing right in front of my door, and I stop so fast that the coffee in my travel mug sloshes over my hand. It's dark. The street is empty. My name is Giselle and I'm sixty-one and I've run this place for twenty-two years and I've never once felt like this, my legs gone weak, a buzzing in my hands, my heart pounding so loudly I'm sure he can hear it. He says, Morning, Giselle. He knows my name. I never told him my name. I back up slowly toward my car, keys bunched between my fingers, never taking my eyes off his face.

Ramón saw the envelope as soon as he pushed the door open, lying on the mat among the weekend's flyers. City Health Department. Inside: a notice that following a complaint of foodborne illness, his taqueria would be inspected today at ten. Below that, a second sheet. Four customers from Saturday had been hospitalized with salmonella. One of them was a child. Ramón's legs went weak. He put a hand on the counter to hold himself up. He thought of Saturday, the delivery of chicken that came late and sat out on the loading dock for who knew how long, the new kid on the prep line who hadn't been trained properly yet. A child. In the hospital. His mouth went sour and he swallowed hard. He thought about his wife, who had mortgaged their house to open this place, about his daughter in her first year at university. He walked to the walk-in cooler and stood in front of it with his hand on the handle, and he could not bring himself to open it and look inside.

Before she even unlocked the hardware store, Bernadette noticed the crack. A long jagged line running up the brick from the foundation to the second-floor window, wider than her thumb, that had definitely not been there on Friday. Over the weekend they had been blasting for the new highway two blocks away. She had felt the windows rattle at home. Now she stood on the sidewalk and stared at that crack, and as she watched, a little trickle of mortar dust sifted down out of it. Her stomach clenched. Her apartment was upstairs. Her nephew Felix, who was staying with her while his parents divorced, was asleep up there right now, right above that second-floor window. Bernadette's keys fell from her hand and clinked on the concrete. She didn't pick them up. She ran around to the side entrance and up the outside stairs two at a time, heart pounding, her own breath roaring in her ears, and she was shouting Felix's name before she had even got the door open.

Eun-ji opened the jewelry shop at nine, as always, and at 9:04 two men in ski masks came through the door. The bell jingled cheerfully. One of them pointed something black at her and said, very quietly, open the cases. Her body did not seem to belong to her. Her hands went up by themselves. Her mouth opened and no sound came out. She had rehearsed this in the training video, cooperate, keep still, press the silent alarm with your knee if you can, but the alarm button was on the other side of the counter and she couldn't move toward it, she couldn't move at all. Her heart was beating so hard and fast that her vision throbbed at the edges. One of the men slammed his palm on the glass, and she jumped and gave a small cry. Her fingers shook so violently she dropped the keys twice trying to unlock the first case. All she could think about was the gun, and her mother's face, and the word cooperate, cooperate, cooperate, repeating in her head like a prayer.

Monday morning, and the first thing I saw when I unlocked the bookshop was the sheriff's notice taped inside the door. Not outside, where anyone could see it. Inside. Which meant someone had been in here with a key. The notice said my lease had been terminated for nonpayment and that the premises had been padlocked. Except it wasn't padlocked; my key had worked. My heart started pounding. I'm Thaddeus and I paid my rent on the first, by check, like always, and I had the bank statement to prove it. Didn't I? I went to the back office and the filing cabinet was open, the drawers pulled out, my records gone. The safe door was ajar. My stomach turned to water. Someone had been here. Someone with keys, someone official or pretending to be, and I had no idea who to call because I had no idea who was doing this. I stood very still in the middle of the dark shop, listening to the building, to the hum of the coolers next door, my pulse thudding in my neck.

Halfway through her shift at the food bank, Annelise looked up from the canned goods table and saw her own mother in the line. Her mother, who lived three hours away. Who had told everyone at Christmas that the business was doing wonderfully. Who was wearing the same coat she'd had for twenty years, now visibly too thin, and was clutching a paper number. Annelise ducked down behind the table, pretending to restock, her heart thundering. What had happened? How bad was it? Was the house gone? Was her mother sick? Was she alone? Each question landed harder than the last. Her fingers fumbled the cans, and one rolled off the table and clanged on the floor, and people turned to look. Annelise crouched there among the boxes of pasta, breathing fast through her mouth, unable to stand up, unable to stay down. She could hear the line shuffling forward. Any second now her mother would reach the table and look straight at her, and Annelise did not know what either of their faces would do.

A man in the line started shouting about forty minutes into my shift. I'm Percival, I'm a retired accountant, I volunteer here Thursdays, and I've seen people get upset before, cranky, sure, tired, sure. This was different. He was yelling that we'd given someone else his share, and his eyes were wild and unfocused, and he was swaying on his feet, and when the coordinator tried to talk to him he swept an entire table of produce onto the floor. Apples rolled everywhere. A child started crying. Then the man reached into his waistband and I saw a handle there. Everything slowed down. My breath stuck in my chest like a swallowed stone. I was standing maybe six feet away, behind the bread table, with nothing between us but a stack of rolls. My knees locked. I couldn't have moved if I wanted to. I just watched his hand, and the handle, and the little girl with her mouth wide open, and I heard someone, very far away, saying call 911, and realized the voice was mine.

The freight elevator in the church basement had been groaning for months, and Ignatius had complained about it twice, but nobody had money to fix it. Tonight he was alone in it with a pallet of donated canned soup, going down, when it lurched, dropped a foot, and stopped dead between floors. The light flickered off and then on again, weaker. Ignatius grabbed the rail with both hands. The cable above him made a long metallic whine, then a snap, then silence. He was seventy-three and he had volunteered at this food bank since his wife died, and he had never once thought about dying in a church basement. Now he could think of nothing else. His heart was racing and skipping. He pressed the emergency button, again and again, his thumb stabbing at it, and heard it ring somewhere far away, unanswered. Everyone else had gone home. Sweat ran down his face. The elevator shifted another inch, groaning, and he pressed himself into the corner, his eyes squeezed shut, gripping the rail so hard his wrists ached.

I was sorting donated jars when the volunteer coordinator mentioned, casually, that ICE had been parked outside the food bank on Tuesday, watching people come and go. She said it like a piece of gossip. I kept sorting, but my hands slowed, then stopped. I come here every week, not only to volunteer but because the volunteers can take home what's left at the end of the night, and that's how I've been feeding my two kids since my hours got cut. My papers expired in 2021. My name is Esmeralda and nobody here knows that. My heart had started pounding and a hot flush crept up my neck. I looked toward the windows. A white van was parked across the street. Was it the same one? Was it a plumber? I couldn't tell. My mouth went dry. The coordinator was saying something about a new shift schedule, and I nodded, and I didn't hear a word. When I put the next jar down on the shelf it rattled against the metal because my hand wouldn't stop trembling.

Sixteen-year-old Leilani had signed up to volunteer at the food bank for her community service hours, and the coordinator had put her on intake, writing down names and addresses, and the fourth person in line gave her own address. Her family's address. But it wasn't her family. It was a man she had never seen before, grizzled and smelling of smoke, who said he'd been living there, in the shed out back, for about a month. Said it as if it were nothing. Leilani's pen stopped moving. Her little brothers played in that backyard every afternoon. Her bedroom window faced that shed. Some nights she had heard sounds out there, and her mom had said raccoons. The man was watching her face now with a small, interested smile. Leilani's whole body went cold, then hot. She tried to write the address down normally and her handwriting came out a wobbling scrawl. She told him to have a nice day. Her voice was a whisper. As soon as he walked away she dropped the pen and ran to the bathroom and locked herself in.

Cornelius had only been volunteering for two weeks when the old woman at the front of the line collapsed. One moment she was taking a bag of rice from his hands, and the next her eyes rolled back and she folded straight down onto the linoleum, the rice bursting open and scattering everywhere. She wasn't breathing. Cornelius knew she wasn't breathing because he was on his knees beside her with his ear to her face, and there was nothing. The other volunteers were screaming for someone to call 911. Someone shouted, does anyone know CPR? And Cornelius did, technically, from a class eight years ago, and his hands hovered over her chest and wouldn't come down. What if he broke her ribs? What if he did it wrong and she died because of him? His heart was hammering so violently that he felt sick. Sweat dripped off his nose onto her cardigan. Somebody said his name. He laced his fingers together, they were shaking terribly, and pressed down, and felt something crack under his palms, and nearly vomited, and kept going.

The surgery was supposed to take two hours. It had been five. Josefina had watched every family that came in after her get called back, one by one, a surgeon in scrubs appearing at the door with a smile, a handshake, and she was still sitting in the same plastic chair by the vending machine. Her husband was in there. The status board on the wall had his patient number in yellow, which meant in progress, and it had been yellow for so long that she had started to hate the color. Her coffee had gone cold hours ago. Her fingers kept worrying the strap of her purse until the leather began to fray. Every time the double doors swung open her whole body jerked upright and her heart slammed. When a nurse came out and looked at her clipboard and then looked directly at Josefina, and did not smile, the floor seemed to drop out from under the chair. Josefina tried to stand and her legs would not hold her, and she sat back down hard.

The man across from me in the emergency waiting room has been coughing blood into a napkin for twenty minutes. Nobody's taking him back. Nobody's taking me back either, and I've been holding my two-year-old, Ines, against my chest for three hours now while her fever climbs. She's stopped crying, which is worse than the crying. She just lies there, heavy and hot, her eyes half open, not tracking anything. Every so often her whole body twitches. I keep pressing my lips to her forehead and every time it's hotter. I went up to the desk twice and the nurse said they're triaging, ma'am, please sit down, and the second time she didn't even look up. I'm Margarethe. I'm a lawyer. I argue for a living. And I couldn't find a single word, just stood there with my mouth open and my throat closed. My arms are shaking from holding her and I won't put her down. I keep watching her chest to make sure it's still rising, counting each breath, losing count, starting again.

It was the police officers that made Jamal's twin brother, Hakeem, go cold. Two of them, standing at the nurses' station in the ICU waiting area, talking quietly with a doctor and glancing his way. Hakeem had brought Jamal in an hour ago with a gunshot wound to the shoulder. Jamal had said it was a robbery. Jamal had said a lot of things. Now the officers were walking over, and one of them had his notebook out, and Hakeem's palms went slick against his jeans. He hadn't seen anything. He didn't know anything. But he knew his brother, and he knew who his brother ran with, and he knew what happened to people in their neighborhood who talked to police. His heartbeat thudded in his ears. The officer asked if he was the brother. Hakeem nodded, his throat too tight to speak. The officer asked if he could answer a few questions. Hakeem looked toward the double doors behind which his brother lay, and toward the exit, and back again, and his knee began bouncing uncontrollably.

They told me the doctor would come out to talk to us as soon as Papa was stable. Stable. I keep turning the word over. It's been ninety minutes since the ambulance, since I found him on the kitchen floor with the left side of his face drooping and his words coming out slurred and wrong. I'm Ishaan, I'm nineteen, I'm the one who called. My mother is in Mumbai visiting her sister; I've texted her but it's three in the morning there and she hasn't answered. It's just me in this room with its bolted-down chairs and its muted TV playing a cooking show. I can't sit. I keep pacing from the window to the water fountain and back. My chest is tight and my hands are freezing and I keep rubbing them together. Every time I hear footsteps in the hall I stop dead. What if he can't talk anymore? What if he doesn't know me? I press my forehead against the cool glass of the window, my breath fogging it, and squeeze my eyes shut and try to stop shaking.

Winifred was not waiting for anyone. She was waiting for her own name. The radiologist had seen something on the mammogram and sent her straight down for an ultrasound and then told her to wait here, in this little side room with the floral curtains and the box of tissues placed rather too prominently on the coffee table. Nobody had told her what they'd seen. Nobody had told her anything at all. She was seventy, she had buried a husband and a sister, and she had thought she was past being undone by a waiting room. She was wrong. Her heart was racing in an odd fluttering way. She kept smoothing the hospital gown over her knees, smoothing and smoothing, as if it had wrinkles. Every time someone passed in the corridor she held her breath. Her mouth tasted of metal. When at last a young doctor came in and closed the door behind him, quietly, carefully, and then pulled up a chair to sit at her level, Winifred's hands went still in her lap and the blood roared in her ears.

The plane crash had been on every channel since noon, and the airline had sent the families here, to the hospital, to a conference room turned into a waiting area with cheap pastries and a coffee urn nobody touched. Survivors were being brought in. Some of them. A list was being compiled. That was all anyone knew. Aurelio sat with his elbows on his knees and his phone gripped in both hands, his daughter's last text still on the screen: boarding! see u soon dad. He had read it perhaps two hundred times. Around him a woman was rocking in her chair and humming. A man was pacing, muttering into his phone. Aurelio's stomach had knotted so tightly he couldn't sit up straight. His jaw ached from clenching. Every time the door opened and an official walked in with a clipboard, the whole room went still, every head turning, and Aurelio's heart lurched up into his throat and stayed there, beating, while the official read out names that were not hers, not yet, not yet.
